utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, I made a mistake. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, Mr. President. We've had a reshuffling of the witnesses during the weekend and this witness is General Dragomir Keserovic, who will be followed by Radomir Pasic. We informed the Chamber a few times by e-mail and the order for today will be General Keserovic followed by Mr. Pasic and Mr. Bajagic, and Ceklic will testify tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Keserovic, my apologies. The Chamber hasn't been informed. In particular I wasn't informed of the recent change of the order of witnesses. My apologies again. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Sorry to interrupt. I believe we had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll discuss it in the absence of the witness. Mr. Keserovic, the Chamber has something to discuss in your absence. If you could excuse us for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I apologise if I'm wrong, but I believe we had suggested that this witness ought to be advised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We noted it, but I was wondering why an expert witness needs a Rule 90(E) advisory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because part of my cross-examination will very likely focus on his whereabouts and actions in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll deal with it when it arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was the understanding of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll bring in the witness again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your expert report, we have your CV, but I would kindly ask you to tell us first where and when you were born and then give us a brief resume of your career, educational background, and career.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 8th of June, 1957, in Piskavica near Banja Luka in the then-Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is where I finished my elementary school, and I finished secondary school in Banja Luka. I finished the military academy of ground forces in Belgrade in 1981. I also finished the General Staff Academy in Belgrade in 1997, and the School of National Defence in 1999 in Belgrade. I acquired my Masters Degree and my Ph.D. at the Faculty of Security, and I teach security sciences. During my military career, I discharged all duties starting from platoon commander, company commander, battalion commander, brigade commander, chief of the corps staff, and in the security service I discharged all duties starting from an operations officer, chief of section, chief of department, chief of administration, chief of the sector for intelligence and security, assistant Chief of the General Staff, and assistant minister for defence. As I said, I currently teach at the University of Security as an associate professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether or not all in the period after 1992 but throughout your career receive any commendations and any decorations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On several occasions I received fast-track promotions and I was decorated as a member of the Yugoslav People's Army, that is to say before the conflict in the former Yugoslavia and later as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your terms of reference as an expert was to review and analyse the expert report provided by the Prosecution witness Ewan Brown relating to the 1st Krajina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have to wait a little bit for the interpretation to be completed and recorded in the transcript. Let me go briefly through the subjects as put in an order in your expert report. Can you tell us what did Mr. Brown conclude regarding the connection between the Serbian Democratic Party and the JNA and the 5th Corps in particular, and what were your conclusions on that very same subject?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In my expert -- in his expert report, Mr. Brown concluded that the Yugoslav People's Army and the Serbian Democratic Party jointly and in co-ordination acted with a view to creating conditions in which Serbs will separate from the other two ethnic communities. He also concluded that through forcible relocation and ethnic cleansing the number of non-Serbs in that territory would be reduced to a negligible number. I believe that that was a very lightly made statement, because after reviewing the same documents as Mr. Brown did, I found that the JNA and the 5th Corps of the JNA and later the 1st Krajina Corps did everything through a long period of time to calm down the situation, to keep it under control, to ensure protection for all ethnic communities, which means both the non-Serbs and Serbs -- and that their attitude depended solely on the attitude that was displayed towards them whenever and wherever the JNA that at the time was the only legal and legitimate armed force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, if it was not attacked, if its soldiers were not being killed or wounded, if they were not put under blockade, they provided equal protection to everyone. Their only response was in a situation when they needed to defend and protect their troops from attacks. That's the essential difference between my findings based on the documents compared to Mr. Brown's findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a member of the JNA, was it possible for you to reach a conclusion about the attitude of the JNA towards nationalist political parties? What was their general view of the so-called ethno-democracy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this witness an expert or a fact witness, Mr. Karadzic? You are asking the witness based upon his experience as a member of the JNA. I'm struggling to understand what this witness is testifying about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I think that on the basis of his review of the documents would be helpful and useful, but I will now stick to the documents solely, and I will rephrase my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please bear in mind that this witness is an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did you come across any documents that were -- corroborate the closeness of views and in particular political views between the JNA and the SDS, and did you find any evidence in documents that JNA had some preferences with regard to political parties both before and during the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not find any such documents that would indicate to pre-war closeness between any nationalist party and the JNA. On the contrary, what I found was a lot of documents that spoke in favour of the fact that the JNA was opposed to ethnic polarisation and was advocating a political solution to these differences. As a result, they called upon everyone to solve the crisis that emerged and the events relating to the disintegration of the former state without a war, that is to say without the use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you come across any documents speaking about the relationship between the SDS and the JNA and how they treated them? Did you find any fact there was total trust between them? And I'm talking about period before the war. What was the attitude of the SDS in general and on the ground vis-a-vis the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party was not particularly trustful, because that was particularly prominent in its right wing. As I said, was mistrustful of the Yugoslav People's Army. They believed them to be the remnant of the previous Communist regime and system, and it could not have anticipated and predicted how the JNA would act in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I could intervene, Mr. Karadzic. In your answer to Mr. Karadzic's previous question, you answered that you didn't find any -- such document that would indicate to pre-war closeness between any nationalist party and the JNA. Do you remember having said so, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, pre-war closeness. Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you mean that attitude changed during the war? Yes. Do you mean that such attitude changed during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Karadzic's questions related to the pre-war period, but with time there would come a period when there was more closeness between the SDS and closeness due to the fact that the remaining two ethnic communities would openly attack and practically push them into the SDS who had never been advocating attacks on the soldiers and the barracks even though initially they were not very trustful of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These documents, do they provide sufficient reason to conclude and explain the reasons why the JNA was relocating its resources, its equipment, weapons, and ammunition to predominantly Serb-populated areas?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It is important to follow parallel -- two parallel processes. One of them relates to the strategic development and deployment of armed forces that had been established long before the conflict started in the former Yugoslavia. The units were mostly deployed in the areas that actually they recruited conscripts from. The other process that ran parallel took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was based on the previous experiences of armed conflict, primarily in Croatia but in Slovenia as well, where the JNA units had been blocked, surrounded, attacked, where weapons were snatched from them as well as equipment and soldiers were taken prisoner. Before the conflict broke out, while the JNA was still in existence, the General Staff issued an instruction or an order for all the areas where it was not certain that the units may survive and that they would be safe that they should be relocated to safer areas. This instruction did not specify areas with regard and on the basis on any ethnic majority. It, rather, dealt with the fact that a situation might occur that as a result of tensions the JNA unit might again become subject of attacks and confiscation of their equipment and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. No objection. It's just there have been some questions about before the war and before the conflict, and I just don't know if it might be helpful to know what the date is and if -- and if that means the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you help us General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are a number of crucial dates that pertain to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The first relate to the month of March when the armed forces of the neighbouring Republic of Croatia entered the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the area of Kupres and Posavina, and that is when they started occupying parts of that area. The next important dates were when the then-president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, in early April and immediately thereafter the commander of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Hasan Efendic, in the period up to 10th of April called upon blockades to be placed on the JNA units and garrison preventing the movement of the JNA and exposing them to attacks in general. Once JNA came under attacks, they responded. And then these attacks started on the 2nd of May in Skenderija, 3rd of May, Dobrovoljacka Street, 15/16 of May in Tuzla, and so on and so forth. The next important date had to do with the fact that in early May, a decision was adopted for the JNA to leave the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that this withdrawal should have been completed by the 19th of May. And finally, on the 20th of June, president of the then-Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued a document declaring a state of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are the dates that I believe could be taken as benchmark that would define the period, the pre-conflict and during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we leave it there, Mr. Nicholls, for the moment? Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, a war is not declared to an unknown enemy. As far as the Muslim and Croatian authorities were concerned, who did they identify as the enemy? Against whom was a state of war declared?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: A state of war was declared against a third ethnic community, that is to say the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was preceded with the war declared on erstwhile joint armed force, that is to say the JNA. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about another topic now from your report. How did Mr. Brown regard the organisation of the non-Serb forces, that is to say the armed forces of the Muslims and Croats in the territory of Republika Srpska? Can you explain to us, please, to what extent did you conclude and on the basis of what that Mr. Brown downplayed that aspect and cited and described certain groups and incidents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown dealt extensively with the military organisation of the Muslims and Croats in what was Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. He addressed in quite some detail the incidents unfolding in certain areas as well. It may be important to note on this score that none of the events unfolding in whatever municipality were accidental. This is not the subject of the analysis but is important to comprehend the events. In early April, as early as that, the first documents issued and the first actions mounted served to the Muslim leadership in Sarajevo to incendiate Sarajevo as well as the Drina valley, Foca, Visegrad, across Zvornik, all the way to Bijeljina, to incense the entire area in order to isolate Bosnia-Herzegovina with respect to Serbia. Next in May and early June it was the Sana valley, Kljuc, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, all these municipalities followed next. Mr. Brown referred to many documents in his report that I, too, reviewed. He states specifically a text and says an attack was mounted, seven members of the JNA were killed who were retreating through Kljuc unarmed. Or another one, at a check-point fire was opened at a military police patrol where three MPs were killed, or seven members of the army were taken prisoner. He does not suppress or conceal these incidents. He does not omit to mention them. However, what was in my view inappropriate was that he kept using terminology that wanted to downplay the whole situation, that this was only few people, that these were minor incidents, that only a few people were killed or taken prisoner, and that it all happened sporadically. As I myself analysed these same documents, I can say that these incidents were initial incidents or were triggers which prompted a response first by the JNA and later by the VRS to these very same events. After all, World War I was triggered by the assassination of the heir apparent with the death of two people. So we cannot say that these were minor incidents, sporadic incidents of little importance which as such prompted such a fierce response. So I do consider such an analysis on the part of Mr. Brown to be inappropriate. If you analyse these events you will see that there is a cause-and-effect relationship. Secondly the use of forces, the strength of these forces, reciprocity, all these issues, of course, can be discussed. However, what I can conclude is that the incidents and later significant events in these municipalities were for the most part initiated, motivated, provoked by these same actions that the Muslims mounted in the various municipalities and which were for the most part directed against the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, sorry to intervene once again. Going back to your career, General, I just took a look into your CV which is included in your report, but I couldn't find what specific post that you took during the war. Could you tell us what you had done since 1991, specific position in which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Well, I was at the General Staff Academy in Belgrade when the war commenced. When the war broke out, I interrupted my schooling and became commander of the armoured battalion of the 2nd Mechanised Guard Brigade in Valjevo. I was part of that brigade when it was deployed in Eastern Slavonija, in Croatia. When I -- when the area was handed over to UNPROFOR --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was part of the JNA, your brigade in Valjevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes, that was part of the JNA. I joined the VRS on the 17th of June, 1992, when we handed over our area of responsibility to the peace forces, that is to say UNPROFOR. That was the unprotected area in east Slavonia. Then I was appointed chief of security of the 329th or, rather, the 1st Armoured Brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps, and I stayed there until September of 1992, at which point I took up the position of the MP battalion commander of the East Bosnia Corps in Bijeljina. I stayed in that position until October of 1993. At the time, I -- or, rather, between October 1993 and February 1995, I was commander of the MP battalion of the 1st Krajina Corps. Between February and late September 1995, I was chief of the MP department in the Main Staff of the VRS, and from early October up until the end of the war I was the commander of the armoured brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And when were you promoted to a general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 9th of January, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now that we're on this issue, General, in the armies in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did the continuation of a military career require certification or approval by the international community which ran a background check in terms of the war path of any senior officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In the VRS -- or, rather, in -- I stayed in the Ministry of Defence up until the 30th of June, 2004. At a time when the defence system embark on a reform before the creation of what is the system of the armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina today, I stopped working in the Ministry of Defence. Now, a requirement that existed as part of that reform, if this is what the question was about was that no senior officer or wartime commander should remain within that new body of defence forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come back to that issue of the degree and the significance of the incidents that you discussed previously. In footnote 2, you mention the decision of the Presidency of the Bosnia-Herzegovina to declare a state of war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness then please be shown 65 ter 05867 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, General, you said between February and September 1995, you were the chief of military police department in the Main Staff. Is that part the one headed by Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was chief of military police department which was within the security administration of the security department -- of the security and intelligence department, and Colonel Beara was the head of the administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the document published in the Bosnia-Herzegovina Official Gazette which you referred to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 20th of June. If you scroll the document down, you will see that it's the 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection. I thought it already was in a different form perhaps, but no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3820, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your report, you state that not just the Muslims and Croats left the ranks of the JNA but also the Serbs who did not hail from Bosnia-Herzegovina. You cite one information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 65 ter 07855 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the document you cite in your document -- in your report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I think that there must be another document dated the 4th of May, but this document also discusses the need to -- for the JNA to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina and for a decision to be taken to that effect. I think that this is a decision issued by the BH Presidency which had yet to be brought in line with the federal level. At any rate, these documents are unique in terms of the subject matter they deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3821, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to note there appears to be a typo on the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In English translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also confirmed that this early relocation of properties meant that they -- or, rather, that they were motivated by the fact that they wanted to be moved to safer areas.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 65 ter 17766 to that effect. This is the cover page. Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the document you meant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the document says, please? You don't have to read, but can you just summarise for us these five points.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This plan of relocation of units from crisis areas in the area of responsibility of the 5th Corps is something that follows the order issued by the 2nd military district which was headquartered in Sarajevo at the time. This plan was to set out new garrisons for certain units. It was said that the relocation would be directed by the corps and that the plan of relocation as well as the routes to be taken would be defined in a separate plan. They were supposed to choose those routes where -- which were not under threat from any possible attacks. International observers are called to come and observe the process of relocation of these units. What this meant simply was a reorganisation of the garrisons and areas the units were supposed to be deployed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3822, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also, you referred to an incident which happened in Dobrovoljacka Street. Actually, it was an event in Dobrovoljacka Street when a JNA soldier was killed by Mr. Izetbegovic's forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 01260, 1D01260.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of May, is that a document that you referred to? What is that document about? Can you tell us about the subtitle and bullet point 1?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This is an analytical document which was issued by the 4th Corps. It lists developments or string of events in Bosnia-Herzegovina during a certain period of time. The document points to the fact that the situation was constantly aggravated, that the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was disastrous, that unfortunately some previous predictions had come true, and that is that the intensity of attacks against the JNA would increase and that the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not care about a peaceful solution of the crisis that had occurred. They were inspired by the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina by some state members of the international community, and they would try to create a Bosnia and Herzegovina according to their own will and that they would continue to fight for that. One of the ways of that struggle would be constant attacks against army units. Dobrovoljacka Street and the attack against Skenderija had one thing in common. Both attacks were carried out, although a peaceful withdrawal of the troops had been agreed. This shows that mistrust spread and continues to spread even further. If even the things that had been agreed cannot be implemented there could be no discussion of any trust in the future. All of that shows that the situation was becoming more and more complicated and that the larger scale conflict was imminent. This is an overview of events which was done by the command of the 4th Corps in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read the one sentence but last under bullet point 2 where it says, "Relocated numerous units, lethal and other MTS to secure areas and locations." Does it say here who would settle those secure areas? Was that more important to the JNA than security itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. There is no document which says what those areas were and who was to settle those areas. I didn't find that in any of the documents. What mattered to the JNA was to preserve and protect both people and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber where was the 4th Corps deployed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Corps was deployed in Sarajevo. It was moved from either Croatia or Slovenia and ended up in Sarajevo. That's where several units were merged. Some of its units were moved from the areas of previous combat activities. However, as far as I can remember, the 4th Corps was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3823, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about the relocation of units, Mr. Brown also dedicated a lot of room to that. Can you please tell us, how did he interpret the relocation of units, for example, to Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kotor Varos? He particularly emphasises Bosnian Krajina, because he dealt with the 1st Krajina Corps. How did he interpret that relocation, and what was your conclusion by contrast?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown spent a lot of time on the relocation of units. His analysis of the relocation of units led to a conclusion that units were relocated to areas where they would be used against non-Serbs, which certainly wasn't correct. He mentions those units as being the 22nd Light Infantry Brigade Skender Vakuf, the 6th Crna Brigade, the 17th Kljuc Brigade, the 43rd Motorised Brigade, the 5th Partisan Brigade Prijedor as well. After they accomplished their mission in Western Slavonia where they were engaged according to the plan of the then-JNA, i.e., the federal state or the former SFRY, they returned to their peacetime garrisons, and Mr. Brown claims that they were relocated to areas where they would be used against non-Serbs. All those units were mobilised in those very areas and in those garrisons to which they finally returned. None of them went to a different area. We're talking about military conscripts, about people who were from those areas, who were mobilised there, who constituted those units and ones that accomplished their missions, they simply returned to the territories of their respective municipalities. There is nothing here that was planned in advance. They did not arrive in those areas in view of some future tasks that they would carry out. The fact is that they were not fully demobilised, because tensions kept on mounting and the situation was continued to get more complicated in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were the base garrisons of those units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The base garrison of the 43rd and 45 Kozara Brigade were in Prijedor; the 6th Light Infantry Brigade was headquartered in Sanski Most; the 22nd was headquartered in Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at 65 ter 017811.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 17811.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about the contents of this document. What is this document about? 18 March 1992, under bullet point 2 you see a reference being made to the changeover of the 122nd?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a combat report of the command of the 5th Corps of the JNA. Later on that will become the 1st Corps. That was sent to the superior command, and it speaks about the regular changeover of units that were deployed in Western Slavonia. One of them was the 122nd Light Infantry Brigade which was replaced by another unit, whereas the former brigade was sent to its base in Skender Vakuf. When we're talking about this brigade, it also had a battalion which was mobilised in the territory of Kotor Varos municipality. In other words, its troops were mobilised in two municipalities plus Celinac. However, its base garrison was in Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3824, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, Mr. Brown also speaks and uses the claim about the take-over of power in the municipalities in Krajina. Could you please tell us who was in power in the municipalities in Krajina before conflicts broke out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The first multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina resulted in the setting up of power based on the election results. The election results brought into power three ethnically based parties: The Serbian Democratic Party, the Croatian Democratic Union, and the Party of Democratic Action. Where the -- one ethnic group prevailed, that ethnic group had a majority in the assembly, and they set up civilian authorities. There was such municipalities where coalition agreements were signed so power was shared -- or, rather, participation in power was in reciprocity with the result by the three ethnically based parties, and there was also a fourth option, the alliance of reform force. In Kotor Varos, for example, the president of the municipality was a Croat, the president of the assembly was a Serb, and the rest of the officials belonged to all the other parties. In any case, power was held by those who won that power in the election. So we can't talk about any take-over of power because there were multi-party elections and powers were given to the parties that won in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the breakout of conflicts, did the authorities change or was the authority uninterrupted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: There were attempts at places to rearrange the majority in the assembly. However, there was a continuity of power during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when we're talking about minor incidents --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P03662. It's a Prosecutor's document, 03662.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What were the daily losses as a result of minor incidents, and how many daily losses are acceptable in a minor incident? Can there be casualties after such minor incidents? Would that be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Obviously it is not acceptable to have an armed conflict or an armed incident. If we use the term "incident," we can only imply a little argument, a skirmish, a verbal conflict, some minor arguments in any case. However, the use of weapons which results in a loss of life cannot be seen as a sporadic incident. Every single human life is too valuable to be seen as the result of a minor incidents, especially if it's not expected. It is expected that there will be casualties in fighting, in an armed conflict. However, deep in the depth of the territory which is not affected by armed conflicts incidents with the loss of human life are unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at page 7 where it says "Losses." You are familiar with the structure of combat reports. Actually, it's on page 3, bullet point 7. "Losses," bullet point 7. Could you comment upon bullet point 7 which speaks of casualties on the 30th and the 31st of May, 1992. How many losses were there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Those events happened in Prijedor. At that time, Muslim forces organised themselves and attacked the town of Prijedor itself and all the institutions of power. They attacked the assembly building, the police station, the garrison. They entered the very centre of Prijedor and as we can see in this report, the 343rd Motorised Brigade alone had 11 members killed and 16 wounded. As far as I can remember, that was not the final outcome. The final casualty number was higher. These are major losses. Therefore, one cannot call this event a sporadic or a minor incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A while ago you said that all of this was happening deep into the territory behind the lines which should not have been a war zone. Can you tell me how far was the front line -- was from the place where these incidents took -- took place? They were several hundred kilometres to the north or to the south, for example.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The initial conflicts and the first actions would create a situation in which certain areas were organised in such a manner that one might say these are the Serb areas, these are the Muslim areas, or as I called them today, Bosniak and these are the Croat ethnic areas. So in the spring of 1992, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was established an exceptionally long front line of forces positioned along such a line. Later on it would become a proper front line that would coincide with the boundaries delineating majority ethnic communities. Now, as for -- as far as the distance between Prijedor and the area controlled by the Muslim forces in Cazin Krajina, if you take the shortest route was between 70 or 80 kilometres. In other words, those were the closest Muslim positions to Prijedor. The next ones would be the positions facing Livno occupied by the Croatian forces and they were even further than the previous ones. So there is no proximity between the positions where combat activity was taking place and the town of Prijedor itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You also focused your attention on what Mr. Brown said about the relationship between our authorities and military commands or their attitude toward minorities and individuals who committed crimes against minority people. Based on the same documents, what was your conclusion with regard to the attitude of the 1st Krajina Corps, and were they open to co-operation with international organisations, and did they co-operate in preventing further conflicts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, General. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The witness may be able to break that down and answer it, but there's a huge amount of concepts in that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's better to break down your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did Mr. Brown characterise the position of the 1st Krajina Corps with regard to the perpetrators and crimes committed against minorities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In his report, Mr. Brown alleges that the corps was aware or had reason to be aware that crimes were being committed against non-Serbs in the area the corps and that it did not do enough to prevent that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your conclusion? But before that, sorry, did Mr. Brown find any proof apart from the passivity that the 1st Krajina Corps issued active orders for crimes to be committed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: He didn't find a single paragraph in a single document that would speak about corps actively insentivising the commission of crimes against non-Serbs. What he failed to do, or at least did not include in his report, even though he even made references to this particular paragraph, was that he ignored the efforts and the continuity of orders demanding measures to be taken explicitly for non-Serbs to be afforded protection, their lives and their property. There is a series of documents that speck in favour of that. However, one cannot dispute that incidents did happen but an analysis based on the facts show that was not an official policy pursued by the corps command and that the command and the corps made every effort to pre-empt such behaviour and if they happened to punish the -- the offenders.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can would please have 65 ter 024 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 04201.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, what was the effect of the behaviour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to appear, can you tell us how the existence of armed forces, non-Serb armed forces that even Mr. Brown recognised in our territory, did they have any effect? Did they prove any threat to our population?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Most definitely. According to the rules of combat engagement of units, any appearance of hostile armed formations deep behind the lines, and that is to say behind the bulk of the forces deployed somewhere on a distant front line requires an action per se. There is no doubt that this presence instills fear and anxiety among the population, and they're even compelled to move out, to relocate, and, quite simply, to leave. In the theory of warfare, that is qualified as rear combat of the enemy if you speak from the point of view of one side and on the other side perceive -- perceives this as a combat with enemy forces that penetrated their territory deep behind the lines. Now, the policy is to neutralise such forces whether by destroying them or capturing them or forcing them to lay down their arms. At any rate, this is a question that is of the highest priority in terms of findings a solution, because it poses a danger that can entail serious consequences. It is important to say that there is something that can additionally make the situation more complex, and that is to say that even back in 1991 and in early 1992, JNA units were far away in Croatia while at the same time the Muslim and Croatia forces were establishing their paramilitary formations. That in itself caused anxiety and uncertainty. The 400 -- the 243rd Brigade would embark on opening a corridor which is 200 kilometres from Prijedor, and they will end up at the Gradacac front line. Throughout this whole period deep inside the territory and near their homes, the Muslim formations remained there in Kozara and elsewhere, and posed constant danger. And they were involved, according to Mr. Brown, to minor actions. Now, this is the whole complex issue of uncertainty and fear that were caused by the general situation and atmosphere of what was happening in the Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This document that you refer to in footnote 22, what was the order in this document issued by the Main Staff and then forwarded by the corps command? You don't need to read it all. Just tell us what it pertains to.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This is a report issued by the organ for morale of the 1st Corps and it reiterates the previous documents that were adopted, and they underline again that no revenge should be taken against the population whoever they are, that there must not be any looting or burning. At the same time, it says that all areas and all events should be given unlimited access to the media outlets, international organisations, and representatives of the international community so that they can have an unhindered insight into what was happening in the area. There were already UN observers, representatives of UNPROFOR in the area already, and it was emphasised that all of them must have an unhindered access to all the areas and to cover all the events that they wished to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the importance and significance given to this document by Mr. Brown in his expert report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: He did cite this report, but he, in my opinion, did not perceive it in a proper way. He said that even though there were efforts through certain documents to draw attention to the looting and other wrong-doings targeting non-Serbs, he says that we are not sure that the 1st Corps followed it to the letter and that their intentions to really prevent that were not honest and that they were disingenuous in that. I think that the document says quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3825, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown made reference to the case of Vecici, a Muslim settlement of the in Kotor Varos. Apart from that location, were there any areas where Muslims were concentrated in Kotor Varos? How were they being treated, and did Mr. Brown take into account the general picture about this municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Vecici is an enclave, and that is where conflicts in Kotor Varos happened, because they did not happen in Vecici alone. We said that Kotor Varos was a municipality where there was power sharing between the three ethnic communities: For example, the TO commander at the time was a Muslim; I said that a Croat was the president of the municipality; the president of the assembly was Serb, and so on. Kotor Varos municipality was one of the municipalities that was an ethnically mixed municipality, and there were all kinds of ethnically based settlement. In addition to Vecici, another large place was Vrbanjci. It's a big place populated by Muslims. Then we have Hadrovci, then the villages on the left bank of the Vrbanja River. There were also Croat villages there as well like Bilice. At the very beginning, in June 1992, all these villages surrendered their weapons by first disarming their illegally an armed compatriots and they lived in peace with the Serbs until the end of 1992 when the majority of them decided to the leave the area. A typical example were the villages of Siprage and Krusevo Brdo. Those were the places where several thousand Muslims along with Serbs did not even turn in their weapons. They were not confiscated, but they crossed over the Vlasic plateau, which means that they were not under any special measures of observing, and they were not subject to any actions. What is typical of Kotor Varos municipality is that some very unpleasant, rough, and difficult events took place. When negotiations started about a peaceful resolution for Kotor Varos, the chief of police from the Banja Luka CJB and the chief of security of the 1st Corps were killed on their way back. These two had almost reached a solution, but they were killed on their way back. Then there was an attack and the killing of Serb civilians in Sardari village. Then there was the killing of conscripts who were seen off to join the army on the 17th of August. Now, we have a whole series of events that simply caused the army to resolve that. There was only one problem relating to Vecici, and that was that the people who had weapons ought to surrender them and then leave the area. Some would stay, some would go of their own accord. Now, they refused to surrender their weapons, and I believe that the basic security standard would have been to have them disarmed and that no one could have allowed them to leave and carry their weapons with them. Quite simply, disarming is a basic prerequisite for any disarming and any such actions, and as a result, a lot of conflicts took place in which many residents of Vecici perished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Brown observe that out of all the many Muslim and Croat villages it was only the village of Vecici that clashed and suffered as many victims?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did say that Mr. Brown analysed this particular locality only, and this incident involving Vecici where there were quite a few casualties is presented without an analysis of the run-up to this incident and what were the preceding developments which led to the conflict where they actually perished.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the time, Excellencies. Would this be the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for 30 minutes and resume at 2 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can you tell us how did Mr. Brown illustrate the level information that the JNA and later the 1st Krajina Corps had about the pressure put upon the non-Serb civilian population and their expulsion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In his report, Mr. Brown arrives at the conclusion that the JNA was informed and was therefore aware of the fact that in the AOR of the 1st Krajina Corps there was forcible expulsion of non-Serb inhabitants in the area going on. He states that the 1st Corps and the JNA in general were aware of these developments within the area of responsibility of the corps. He then went on to state that not enough or nothing was done to prevent this forcible resettlement or displacement of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your conclusion that you arrived at on the basis of the same documents that Mr. Brown reviewed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In the early months of the spring, that's to say at the start of the year, we have already the first documents and reports from the 1st Corps and therefore the army which indicate that tension is on the rise and that people started moving out already due to the fact that these tensions might have led to escalations and this definitely caused a feeling of general insecurity among the people. Thus the JNA, primarily the 1st Corps, issued instructions in the form of orders, instructions, et cetera, to their troops that they should protect the entire population. In all the documents without fail they say that protection should be afforded regardless of their ethnic, religious, or any other affiliation, and that efforts should be made to ease the pressure that was brought to bear on the population in terms of their forcible transfer and that their property should be protected. This is the sort of documentation that Mr. Brown had at his disposal and did cite, but his conclusions were of the kind that you described earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 65 ter 08227.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You took in document into consideration, and you cited it under footnote 28. Can you tell us what the 5th Corps command ordered in this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The document addresses the relations with observers, that's to say the UN mission, as well as with the incidents of possible misuse of UN insignia in the area. The document goes on to strictly prohibit any sort of abuse or misuse of the sort, as well as to regulate the co-operation between these various bodies with a view to protecting the population from forcible transfers. It even goes so far as to regulate the exchanges of the fatalities of those killed in combat. It also precisely defines the facts that the convoys used to this effect can only be stopped for identification checks and for no other reason. It's a document which orders in no uncertain terms that the population should be treated positively, as well as the international forces, and regulates that the mortal remains of those killed in clashes should be dealt with proper decorum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a JNA document. 4 April is the date. It was signed by Major-General Momir Talic. Was this sort of practice changed when the 1st Krajina Corps was set up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. It did not change. All the documents that were produced subsequently follow the same lines in regulating the treatment of the civilian population and units, international units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, how did Mr. Brown characterise or qualify this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This document, as well as most of the other documents that Mr. Brown reviewed, were cited in his report. However, they were not given the necessary significance. In other words, in his view the corps and the army units did issue these orders, but he was not fully certain that they intended them to be fully applied. He took isolated events and crimes again the non-Serbs and placed them before the systemic decisions and orders, according them more importance and concluding that this was essentially insufficient, superficial, and was introduced merely so that it may serve as a screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can had been admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3826, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, what sort of weight did Mr. Brown give to the extremist outbursts that took place in certain circumstances, the extremist positions, and did he go on to analyse whether these extremist views were at all incorporated in the documents issued by the Krajina government as well as the Republika Srpska Assembly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer the question, General. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, no objection. I just wonder if this time -- I haven't been asking for cites, but if I could ask for a cite because I don't know exactly what Mr. Karadzic is referring to in Mr. Brown's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me find it. It's the portion where he states that certain individuals made such and such statements. As soon as I find it, I'll cite it. I thought that it was clear. When I find it, I'll let you know the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you observe the attitude that Mr. Brown had vis-a-vis these various statements that could be found in the document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When analysing the course of meetings and sessions and reviewing the minutes, Mr. Brown discerns in them the interventions given by individuals which speak from positions which we could characterise as unacceptable or extremist, extremist in their demands. He translates them into a general position by the Assembly, Presidency, or the government. He presents it in his report as part and parcel of the official policy and as the official position of the organ in question or the Serbian authorities. Following the course of his argument vis-a-vis these documents, I reviewed them but was unable to find that these extremist positions expressed by individuals were in fact translated into official documents such as decisions, instructions, or any other sort of document. These positions were expressed, undoubtedly, but they were not something that resulted in an official position taken along that same line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, again no objection. Is Mr. Karadzic referring to the 16th Assembly session? Is that what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That too. However, Mr. Brown mentions isolated extremist positions stated by ARK officials. These were statements made orally, but he does not go to prove that they were in fact incorporated into the official policy. Of course, both these statements and the documents are something that we need to take into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did Mr. Brown understand the reasons behind the aspirations on the part of the Muslims and Croats to move out, and were there any cases where Serbs were resettling?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats moved out and Mr. Brown treats this in his findings as forcible departure. In some paragraph he also refers to that as ethnic cleansing, which was done under the pressure put on them to bear by the Serbian authorities and that that was the key and main reason why the population decided to move out. What is really significant and what I deem to be significant is the fact that the population mostly moved out because of the fact that in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a conflict had started, a war had started, that there was a state of insecurity that reigned, and everybody tried to leave the area if they at all could do that, all with a view for saving their lives and the lives of their families as well as their property. The overall conditions were the key reasons for people moving out. Why do I consider this to be the fact? Because a large number of Serbs move out from the municipalities in Western Krajina. Militarily able-bodied men stayed behind because they had been mobilised, and they were subject to other laws and responsibilities. However, those who could and who had somewhere to go moved their families out. It was not just the non-Serbs who moved out from Krajina. Everybody moved if they had somewhere to go. The second reason was the economic reason. For several months, Krajina was completely blocked. It didn't have electricity, food, or medicines. Our newborn children were dying in hospitals. So whoever could leave the area wished to go, wished to leave, and that was the key motive of their departure and not somebody's official policy which put pressure on somebody in order to make them leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up 65 ter 00416. For Mr. Nicholls and the other participants in these proceedings, in paragraph 20 of this report, paragraph 2139 from Mr. Brown's report is cited, where it says this is compounded by the public appearances of some leaders of Bosnian Krajina who sent messages over the media advocating the departure of non-Serbs, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you please tell us why this document or this instruction is important.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This is a report by the command of the 1st Corps. We can see that it bears the day 28 July 1992. At the time, combat activities were undergoing, and this shows that at that time, far behind the lines of the troops on the front line there were organised Muslim and Croat forces which were either preparing to carry out activities or were already carrying out activities against the territory behind the lines. At the same time, groups were infiltrated from some other areas, and those areas were under the control of Muslim and Croat forces. Those were sabotage and terrorist groups and units. For example, in the Kotor Varos sector, we had a group that infiltrated from Dobratic in Jajce. It was a very strong group of fighters which was the first Croatian battalion in Kotor Varos. Their goal was to reinforce the forces that were already in the area, linking up with them. This clearly demonstrates that the situation was not stable. It was a neuralgic area where there were still forces very active behind the lines of the main corps forces much deeper into the area behind the lines of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us tell us something about paragraph 3? What did the command observe, and what did they report to the Main Staff about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the activities of extreme groups it is observed that a number of requests for the resettlement of Muslim and Croatian inhabitants were on the rise. This is an ongoing process, and again the main reason were all those activities and the possibility of future conflicts. All that motivated the population to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3827, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this document cited in one of the footnotes of his report, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies. It is in footnote 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If a bar table motion would be acceptable for documents that were used by General Keserovic, it would allow me to finish much sooner. I don't know what the position of the Chamber would be on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the Chamber's position is consistent throughout. Consult with Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We consulted about that, but I told him we couldn't be guaranteed that any of these documents would be admitted through the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up 65 ter 05074.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a while ago we spoke about the extreme position which were expressed by the media. Let us see what you observed, what kind of an official document you came across. Can you tell us something about this document? What is it? It was issued on the 29 May 1992. It was issued by the Crisis Staff of the AR Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be zoomed in a little, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a decision -- or, rather, a conclusion issued by the Crisis Staff of the ARK. The document regulates certain issues which arose from the overall situation. Some appointments are made, and pecuniary sums are determined. I believe that the document should be moved, because the second part of the conclusion concerns more --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the following page where we see the conclusions of the 29 May session. Now we can see it, yes. We missed bullet point 1. However, can you tell us about the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The position of the Crisis Staff was that people who wanted to move out should be allowed to do so. In other words, that the resettlement of the population should be allowed. Those who wanted to leave should be allowed to do so when they express a desire to do that and when creations were created to do that, when they have received an approval by the local communes and when their resettlement was organised. I believe that under bullet point 1, if that is the document that I have in mind, the same -- is says that the same should be allowed to the Serbs who live in the areas under Muslim or Croat control, that there should be a reciprocity in those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you have bullet point 1 before you, and for the participants in Mr. -- or, rather, in General Keserovic's report on page 38 there is a translation of this document in e-court. Unfortunately, we only have the Serbian version. On page 38 you will find the English translation of this document. Yes, this is the bullet point.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This would be an organised exchange of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How would you call resettlement within the same state or within the same municipality or within the same entity? Could that be seen as ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: When it happens within the same municipality or within the same entity or within the same state, resettlement can be carried out. It's even an obligation. It was an obligation on the previous laws. The population from war struck --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will withdraw it, Your Honour. I was thinking these legal conclusions that he was making are a bit beyond the scope, but I'll leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the following page, paragraph 3. The Crisis Staff also decided what? Paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This shows the continuity of official positions of the authorities to decisively counter the attempts of forcible resettlement of the population under duress and that this should be prevented by all means. This is just one in a series of documents that treats what was a very crucial and sensitive issue at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What gained prevalence in Mr. Brown's report, the official document or the unofficial statements by unknown people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Those individual statements prevailed over the official act, and they were used as his grounds for conclusion that forcible resettlement was part of the official policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll mark it for identification pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3828.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sure it is translated, Your Honour. I recognise these documents. I'm looking for the translations with Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it was translated in the report as well in part. Thank you. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did Mr. Brown establish what the position of the 1st Krajina Corps was towards extreme behaviours? Was it lenient? Did the 1st Krajina Corps turn a blind eye to the behaviour of extremists or any kind of extremist behaviour?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown mentions documents issued by the 1st Corps which treat the issue of the corps' attitude towards crime or criminal activities against non-Serbs. However, just like in the rest of his report, he considers this not to be sufficient enough. He considered this to be superficial, and he expresses his doubts about the serious implementation of such decisions even where there are imperatives, demands referred to as terms at all costs, in every possible way. He doesn't find enough reason to deem this to be positive activities on the part of the command of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now comment upon his paragraph 2147 where he says in document dated on the 14th of June that Muslims and Croats are persecuted from Krajina into Central Bosnia but that failed due to difficulties in transportation and the -- and resistance on their part to leave their residence? How did he understand that resistance when unarmed civilian population could put up resistance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The result of that activity, and that was that the activity failed because the civilian population did not want to leave their places of residence, demonstrates that that was not a forcible activity. In other words, that they had a choice and that it was up to them to decide whether they wanted to or whether they didn't want to go to Central Bosnia. If that had been done by force, then the civilian population would not have been in a position to put up any resistance to either the police or the military that wished to expel them. Therefore, this points to the fact that some of those cases demonstrated that the population decided differently and that they were allowed to stay. As far as I can remember, it says in these paragraphs that they would still be guaranteed full protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 65 ter 09415.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what the imperative position was of the 1st Krajina Corps. You yourself mentioned those imperatives and those imperative elements in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I misspoke. The number is 09415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Footnote 37.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. ERN number 00949869. Oh, I'm sorry. But if we cannot have it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, can we please have the next, but it says here that attached here with is the order of the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps. Now, can we move to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a list of all the brigades and subordinate units that received this information, or is any unit missing from the list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I would say that all the units are listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have page 17. "Moral and psychological preparations." Can you tell us what the first four lines are about? Was there any work done with the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see here a list of activities. Each task and each activity is accompanied by numerous preparations, be it material, professional, and also and moral and psychological preparations. The troops are being made aware here about the significance of the task, about all the potential dangers and surprises that might occur. They are invited to carry out their tasks in a conscientious manner, and the commanders are asked to control both the units and their respective zones, to monitor the conduct of their troops, and to react to any contact contrary to the regulations and to what is expected and to send regular reports in that respect. So this is a whole series of preparations, and this kind of psychological preparations always preceded any serious task carried out by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the last page which is item 11. What does item 11 say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Item 11 reiterates in the most stringent way any mistreatment of population and requests the treatment of prisoners in accordance with the spirit of the Geneva Conventions. This is an official position of the corps commander, and this is one of the documents in which this is being emphasised and ordered for the umpteenth time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Brown afford proper evaluation and value to this document in his report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the role of the 1st Corps and the 1st Corps command in the process of providing protection to the civilian population was not properly evaluated. It seems to me that all the effort that they made to provide protection to everybody, all populations regardless of their ethnicity and were not given a prominent place in Mr. Brown's report. I repeat that he gave priority to incidents and criminal offences that undoubtedly did happen, but that was not prevalent conduct and they had never been encouraged or ordered by anyone, and if they happened, they always ended up by discovering the perpetrators and prosecuting them or applying appropriate measures against them. Nevertheless, he laid emphasis and stress on this kind of incidents even though there was a huge number of documents that clearly show how much effort was made by the corps in their area and during the difficulty time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3829, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, was the army involved in preventing inter-ethnic conflicts, and did that have a negative effect on the combat readiness of the corps and its units? Was that something that Mr. Brown noticed, that certain elements were allocated to prevent such conflicts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the whole period and especially 1992, elements of units and even entire units were involved in the activities in the internal area surrounded by front lines. They established organs and regimens and situations that would provide protection for the population living in the area. If some of the elements from the operational units were allocated to carry out activities in the rear -- weakened their combat activity and every other capacity on the front line. However, that was a solution that could not have been avoided and it was not prompted by unjustified reasons or by something beyond that. The sole purpose was to make the area more peaceful and safer. After all, the people everywhere, including in Bosnia-Herzegovina, felt safer if they had army units deployed in certain areas. They would even ask for units not to be sent to the front line or to have them returned from the front line due to the general feeling of insecurity, and of course if the units left certain forces in the rear, that was something that weakened them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 00335, and it has to do with footnote 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, but the question wasn't responsive to the second half of Mr. Karadzic's question which was whether that was something that Mr. Brown noticed in this topic, i.e., was it included in his report. I don't know if Mr. Karadzic wanted an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless I can have a look, I cannot say for sure that he did notice that certain units remained in the zone, but whether he addressed this issue in terms of whether this was something that weakened the units or not, I wouldn't be able to tell you offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this document available to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
