utterances.text: Can you please tell us what this is? The date is the 16th of July, 1992, an order to carry out combat operations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have page 3. It's page 5 in e-court, actually. Can you please look at the last sentence of the first paragraph. Can you finish it? Do you see the last sentence on the first paragraph? The decision, item number 4, which starts, "I decided." Can you read the last sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Let me find it first. In the whole area of operations, prevent at any cost -- throughout the war zone prevent at all cost the creation of new spots and an outbreak of inter-ethnic conflict and prevent genocide of whether it's Serbs or non-Serbs and other people because I can't see it clearly. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe it's Serb and other population?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Serb and other population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 7 in e-court. Second paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be prepared to prevent inter-ethnic conflicts in the territory of Skender Vakuf municipality and genocide between the ethnic groups and the entire population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Only one part is omitted. Have a portion of the forces, does that mean that some elements of the forces would be taken out from combat with the enemy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the forces that were assigned to preventing inter-ethnic conflicts. This is a territorial component which involves the deployment throughout the whole area in order to preempt any inter-ethnic components.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 7 which is page 13 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at item 16 which starts, "After the formation of units." Can you please read the paragraph up to the mention of Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: "... on forming units quickly start strengthening collective spirit and energetically suppress all forms of defeatism, psychopathy, panicking, and other negative manifestations. During combat operations do everything you can to suppress looting in the villages. Before each assignment prepare the troops psychologically for their tasks and while they are carrying out their assignment boost their morale, encourage them and inform them through brave acts of individuals in their own and other units in previous battles. I most strictly forbid mistreatment of the civilian population and captured soldiers must be treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Was this document properly evaluated by Mr. Brown in his report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Not in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3830, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown addressed the issue of property ownership, flats, et cetera. Can you tell us briefly how did he perceive the issue of tenancy right, ownership, private ownership, and what were his conclusions in that respect, and were they correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In his findings, Mr. Brown made an error of law in terms of the laws that were in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, and he put an equation mark between ownership and tenancy rights, which is not the same, far from it. According to the place of work, people were given certain flats and other residences to use, which made them tenants or the holders of tenancy rights. These flats, however, had their owners which were, let's say, government organs, the army, the police, companies, work organisations. They were the ones who built those flats and who were their owners. In order to satisfy certain living standards of their employees, they gave those flats for use. Once the contractual relations between the users of and the owners of the flats ceased, this flat was allocated to someone else, which means the previous tenant did not have the right of ownership, which is something that Mr. Brown either overlooked or just thought it was one and the same thing. As a result, in his report he says that upon departure of the Croats and Muslims, their flats were confiscated and given to be used by someone else. This was simply something that was stemming from the law in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any evidence that there were some unlawful changes of ownership of immovable properties as a result of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The documents that we were able to review, I wasn't able to find anywhere that anyone's property had been taken away unlawfully. The property was placed at the disposal of a certain community, municipality, or the owner. And where housing units were concerned, they were given for use to other vulnerable elements of the population such as refugees. However, when it comes to the change of title deeds there, I did not come across any unlawful activities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] can we look at 00733, a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have a list of abandoned flats. What does "DP Proleter" mean or "Vrbanja"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: They were companies owning these flats. What follows below is a list of holders of tenancy rights. What follows from this is that among those who are on the list of individuals whose flats are vacant, there are Serbs, Muslims, Croats. So everyone is listed here. Everyone abandoned or left these flats behind under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how are these flats treated? Who is able to freely dispose of them? Who is their owner? Is there management on the part of the municipality temporary? Is that a change of title deeds?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. The title deeds remain with the companies or with those who had them built. However, they were temporarily placed at the disposal of municipal authorities in order to provide for the vulnerable elements of the population that we spoke of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's see what this is about. On page 2, item 9, Bahra Drakulovic, two-room apartment currently inhabited by Zdenko Zakan with permission of DSPP Vrbanja. In other words, a Croat moved into a Muslim flat owned by DSPP Vrbanja and it was the SPP Vrbanja that actually handed the flat over to a new tenant. And is this in keeping with the law?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Below it reads DP Rad, Hajrudin Fific [phoen], two-room flat sealed. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It means that at this point in time nobody was granted the right to move into the flat. In other words, the flat would remain vacant until such time as it is assigned to someone according to a priority plan that would be adopted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I note it was referred to in footnote 56 for the record. Shall we assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3831, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 26, you quote paragraph 2154 of Mr. Brown's report where he states that according to General Talic's documents, the army accepted the general policy of separation along ethnic lines and ethnic transfer of population. It would criticise the civilian authorities on occasion for the fact that they failed to fully implement this policy at times, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes we didn't have the original.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 04202 which is footnote 58 in General Keserovic's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was your conclusion of the finding contained in paragraph 5214? Do you have your report with you? Perhaps the Chamber will allow you to use it. It's page 54 in your report. Footnote 58.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This is a situation in an area described here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in both languages with item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you take us through this.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Taking in consideration this document as a whole and specifically item 3 which details the situation on the ground, we can see that there are considerable forces here which are still active in the area of Kozarac and on the slopes of Mount Kozara. These forces continue to be active in the area. In Mr. Brown's analysis, he does not give much importance to this. He doesn't attach much importance to this. Much later after the resolution of the problems that emerged in Prijedor, Kozarac, and the surrounding locations there is still a presence of forces that have not been dealt with fully, that are still active in the rear. These are no small groups. We can see that there's a group of 162 soldiers and that's a significant force which can in the -- make huge problems in the area of the municipality and town of Kozarac itself if we take into consideration that both units normally stationed in Prijedor are deployed far away at the front line at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you observe the fact that Mr. Brown identifies the position that I advanced about the rights of civilians, freedom of movement, and freedom of residence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He does discuss this, but only sporadically and in several parts of the report that you yourself made public, open statements where you emphasised the freedom of movement, where you underlined equal rights for all, where you asked that the population be provided for and that a political resolution of the situation needed to be awaited, which would ultimately come about. Now, these general efforts expressed in a number of documents and statements where you are addressing those who are being the arbiters of peace, who are looting, putting pressure to bear or engaging in unlawful activities, among all these general efforts he only cites this particular one without attaching enough significance to it or analysing it in sufficient details. He merely expresses this general situation, some sort of general policy where ethnic cleansing was to be taking place, where people were to be put pressure upon in order to leave the area, where their property would be taken away. So he is expressing this negative attitude vis-a-vis all your efforts, including yourself personally, in favour of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In footnote 59 you mention some of the documents, two of which are admitted, and in item 3 there is mention of a rogue groups that are actually behaving the way they see fit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3832, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 65 ter 04207. Paragraph 3, which is in the next page. In English as well, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the combat report for 2nd August. The corps is sending it to the Main Staff, and let's see what sort of reports come from the ground. The looting in the liberated areas continues. Civilian authority has not managed to take hold, but there is also mention of the Prijedor region here. Can you tell us what the document says on that score?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It says in the region of Prijedor there is no significant enemy activity or presence. Pressure demands on the part of Muslim and Croats to move out, and their moving out in organised fashion from a general area of Krajina is evermore present, even though some of the emigrants are returning in an organised fashion and getting involved in enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this mean, are fighters coming back or are families coming back?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not include some of these documents in my report. However, when they left these areas for other territories under Muslim or Croat control in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or in certain cases they would go to Croatia or abroad, able bodies persons would come back and join the ranks of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Croatian Defence Council depending on their affiliation, and they re-surface as our adversaries on the front. I did not include these other reports, but there is a number of them where we are confronted with these same individuals over and over again. At one point they would move out of the area, and then at some point we would see them again fighting for the enemy side. In other words, their families would not be coming back, but they would as soldiers and adversaries.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3833, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 00394, 65 ter document. 00394. That should be a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Meanwhile, let me ask you this, General. In document P05407, there is report of capture of paramilitary formations, and it is said that there is 7.000 of them. Two names are mentioned, Zarko and Anto Stanic. Can you tell us why these two names are being singled out? Who are they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Zarko Tole and Anto Stanic were also members of the former army. They are commanders and organisers of Croatian units. Among others, they were taken prisoner in Central Bosnia in combat. They were senior officers. Zarko Tole was lieutenant-colonel at the time. He was the commander of a MP battalion in Sarajevo before the war, and that's how I know him personally. The unit that I was in command of was charged with providing security for him until his exchange. In other words, they are the organisers of Croat units in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And are they professional officers, capable officers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They are graduates of the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We admitted the one before, and this is a wrong document, so let's move on. General, in paragraph 31, you address Brown's paragraphs 2163 -- or, rather, just that one paragraph, which deals with pressure that was being put and with the meetings that were being differently perceived.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 02268.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here the 1st Corps command, Vukelic, say that they received provisional regulations from the Presidency that were adopted; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page. The next page, please. Can we have page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us what this reads? What does this mean that the provisional regulations will be in force as soon as they are adopted? Can we have the next page?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we have page 8, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- can you take us through the document? What is it that members of the army are going to be bound by, and what is it that they will have to adhere to in combat?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: These professional regulations provide that in combat the members of the army would have to adhere to international laws of -- laws of war, that they will have to treat the wounded and captured humanely and protect the population in the combat zone without, of course, singling out anyone in particular from among the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3834, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can we look at 65 ter 1D00254. This is a regular combat report dated 30 March 1993. Look at bullet point 3, please. What is the attitude of the commander -- or, rather, the senior officers towards the Muslim population which is frightened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: A series of reports, including this one, shows that the commanders and units report on all the events and phenomena observed in the territory. They do not omit to say that some irresponsible individuals committed crimes against Muslim population in some villages. They report about that. And later on we will see that they inform the superiors, and they keep on going back to the requirement to act and to exclude irresponsible individuals from their ranks in order to prevent such events. So there was no intent to cover up any of those incidents, on the contrary. Everybody is kept abreast with a view to preventing such actions. This shows that there was a positive attitude towards acting against those who violate the rules of conduct toward the civilian population, i.e., that the civilian population should not be threatened or put pressure upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the following page in Serbian and can we stay on the same page in English. The first paragraph where it says --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: "The command of the 1st Krajina Corps intervened by sending a Military Police Platoon which was supposed to protect the population from irresponsible individuals."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we need the full translation, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I would object to it being admitted in this form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We shall mark it for identification pending full English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3835, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, shall we take a break, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I take it Judge Lattanzi got a little bored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are sitting for the remainder of today pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Lattanzi being away due to her official duties. Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that General Keserovic mentions in footnote 35, which was admitted as 3828, D3828 already has a P number, 3461. Just for the record so that it's clear that the document has been admitted as a P exhibit, and here we have it admitted as a MFI document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That number will be assigned for an upcoming exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to thank you and the Prosecutor for having informed us about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, how did Mr. Brown see the instances of looting and what were your conclusions about that and about the attitude of the army and state organs towards looting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It is true that the looting of property did happen and that it was a common occurrence during armed conflicts. One of the key elements in Mr. Brown's findings was the fact that he looked at the activities of the 1st Corps and the military and concluded that the corps, the military, and the authorities in general countered looting. However, they approved the looting if it was done on behalf of the corps and its coffers as he himself points out. Judging from the documents that we analysed, it is clear that the corps and the military in general, as well as the authorities, unreservedly demanded and did everything in their power to prevent looting of anybody's property. There isn't a single paragraph in a single document which points to the fact that the conduct of individuals who were involved in such actions and activities was condoned. The accompanying documents, i.e., documents that were issued in respect of individuals and groups that looted and plundered were express in their contents. They contained demands upon all units to fight to the last even at the cost of the use of arms in order to prevent that type of activity which obviously inflicted a lot of harm on everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at 65 ter 17877.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the title of this document? It is an order issued by the commander of the 1st Krajina -- or, rather, the 5th Corps on the 14th of May, a week before the withdrawal of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is just one of the documents, one of the orders that was sent to all units in order to prevent plunder and other crimes that might be committed by corps members. This is a strict order as to how they should behave and what measures they should take against those, as you can see under paragraph 2, who are involved in criminal activities. There is a list of those things that need to be done, and the last stages would be arresting them and putting them on trial and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the following page in the Serbian version whereas the English version can stay on the screen as it is. Look at the first paragraph on the second page.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It says here that the most serious methods have to be used against all those. So this is a set of conclusions or actions which need to be taken against perpetrators of all sorts of criminal activities. Should these persons offer resistance during their arrest or attempt to escape, the toughest physical methods should be applied against them, including the use of firearms. This is what it says in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about paragraph 2(b)?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Under 2(b) we can see that this is about preventative activities, that new privates and officers should be vetted before joining the unit in order to prevent potential criminals and those who already have criminal records from joining our units, and those who show propensity towards all sorts of crime, war crime, and who are already in the units, should be removed from those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brown suggests, however, that the looting of property was acceptable as long as rules were honoured and if the goods were put in the coffers of the VRS to be used for the purposes of the military and not for the financial gain of, and so on and so forth. This is paragraph 2, bullet point 186 in his findings. Disregarding individuals, could you please tell us about the measures that Galic and Talic ordered? Did Mr. Brown offer and point to a single document in order to prove that corps units were engaged in the looting of private property for the benefit of the corps coffers as is suggested in here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. There are no such documents that would prove his point that the looting of property was allowed to anybody. What Mr. Brown said here or did here, as it were, is this: He provided an unacceptable interpretation of things that were done with war booty and confused that with the illegal confiscation or looting of property. He put all those documents at the same level in a way, so when it came to regulating the collection and use of war booty, he thought that that was looting for the purpose of the state and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we heard from the minister of defence as to what could be considered as war booty. Under what conditions could private property be confiscated and considered legitimate war booty even if the property had a known owner?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In principle, private property could not be considered war booty. It could be requisitioned. It could be taken and mobilised as part of a legal procedure and it could be used in combat by the military. Some movable goods, primarily could be requisitions or temporarily confiscated and given to use to a particular unit. However, when it comes to private property or private assets, those could not be considered war booty, at least not the kind of war booty envisaged by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at paragraph (c), and can you read the fifth line from the top of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The sentence starts with the following words: "At these meetings, the most prominent officers of the units appear to explain to the population, regardless of their ethnic affiliation, the following things: First, the goals of our struggle; second, intentions of the enemy; three, the tasks of our army; four, what is expecting from the people who live in the area in which we are fighting; and five, negative occurrences that do moral damage to our struggle. Such gatherings should be attend by as many of our soldiers as possible while taking care to ensure the security of the soldiers, units, and population."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read out the first sentence again, (c). Can we see the previous page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At those rallies --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, number one sentence under (c)?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: "Every time you pass through or stay in a populating area, contact local people through local authorities at public rallies, meetings, events and so on."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3828, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 17880.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your paragraph 33 you cite his paragraph 2.171 where he says that on the 17th of May, the corps received yet another order in which it says that they should collect information about soldiers, officers, looting, and so on and so forth, and the police units and crimes that those persons committed. What does it say here in the preamble, and I read, "On the basis of requests from units..." What is it that is requested from units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: At the lowest level requests arrive from privates, from combatants, to counter and fight individuals who plunder in the -- the areas of combat activities. So far we have seen orders that came from the higher echelons of command, and here in this document we can see that individuals are also aware of the dangers that lie in the instances of looting and the damages inflicted thereby on the military and its struggle. That is why they demand that all that should be placed under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have item 10. I believe it's on the next page in both versions. No, I'm sorry, that's not it. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3836, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is suggested in Mr. Brown's findings that officers were discontent having seen that the looted things were confiscated by private individuals and that they were not happy to see it go to the army coffers. Can you tell us what was to be done with the war booty according to the law, and was it possible for it to end up in the coffers of the corps and the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No, that was not possible. War booty was supposed to be disposed of by the state. That is to say the local municipal government, and it was them who disposed of it. Army units captured or seized war booty, and thereafter they would hand it over to the local communes in a proper procedure, that is to say to the local civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from these orders and threats, did the army undertake any other measures with respect to prosecution of the looters and those who misused the power of firearms in order to amass personal wealth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. In addition to the orders issued in all these documents, there were other rules and laws that governed these issues. Military police units had certain organisational parts that were involved in suppressing criminal activities, and all offenders, including war profiteers and other crimes were apprehended by them, processed, and after that handed over either to the military courts or to the civilian courts. Sometimes they launched such operations in co-operation with the civilian police. So there were systematically implemented measures against perpetrators of such crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown document 17866, 65 ter. In the report it's under footnote 71.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what is being ordered by this document. For example, let's start from the third paragraph from the bottom which stipulates the duties of the military police and then where criminal reports should be filed, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This is a document entitled "Actions against violence, looting, and other forms of unlawful conduct." Now, going from the Supreme Command and the Main Staff of the army issued an order to this effect, and it is concluded that the police, military police, and security organs have a duty to undertake measures in order to uncover such acts and identify the perpetrators, whereas the confiscated and other property, money, and proceeds acquired shall be confiscated against a receipt. Criminal reports against the perpetrators are to be filed with relevant military prosecutor offices which in war were attached to the command of corps. As for military prosecutor offices attached to the Main Staff of the army, it involves the Military Court in Banja Luka, and it says that it will start operating. So what you can see here is already a kind of organised approach which is paving the way for criminal reports to be filed against perpetrators with the courts that were in the process of emerging and starting to become operational at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What you said a minute ago, that it is to be handed over to the state organs, in the prosecutor's document 502.2, that all the movable property seized during the war shall be handed over by the VRS to the relevant municipal or republican organs. Is that what you had in mind when you said that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3837, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2181, Mr. Brown discusses a receipt that is issued according to the instruction, and he explains that: "This receipt is viewed in the context of a decision which limits the amount of money that those leaving the territory could take with them, the handing over of housing to the Serb municipal authorities and the signing of documents of deregistration. It is clear that an organised and systematic process was adopted by which the non-Serbs would not only be removed from their place of residence and be unable to return but by which their property would be taken from them with the intention of it being placed in the Bosnian Serb coffers for use and the funding of the new Bosnian Serb state." Can you first tell us what was it that you find with regard to the limiting of monies that can be taken out of the territory? How was it regulated by the law then and now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The laws, or, rather, the fiscal policy of each state with the exception of between states who are sort of monetary unions, strictly defined the amount of cash that an individual can take out of the country. At the time, this amount was 300 German marks, that is to say that each individual was allowed to take from the former Yugoslavia or from Bosnia-Herzegovina. And by this instruction this was only emphasised once again. There was no other reason for imposing a limit in this sense. Equally, what Mr. Brown failed to evaluate properly, this is to do only with 300 German marks that cannot be shown the origin of. This is pocket money of an individual. Regardless of the amount that exceeds this one, if a person has proper documents confirming that it had been purchased from a bank or that it was the proceeds of the sale of property, this person was allowed to take out this amount of money. The only limitation referred to the money whose origin was not proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the current situation now? What are the rules now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the rules are the same, only the amount has been increased slightly. A person can take out of Bosnia-Herzegovina 5.000 euros and that's maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 17871. Page 2, because in paragraph 2181, Mr. Brown speaks about the fact that the seized property was stored in the government coffers, including small pieces of furniture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us how these items from the list could have arrived at the storehouse for war booty -- or, rather, the storehouse for unlawfully possessed merchandise?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This kind of merchandise, according to the instruction, was most probably seized from individuals who had previously misappropriated it in an unlawful way. Then when they arrived at check-points and searched, these items were confiscated from them as unlawfully plundered and was placed in the depots together with war booty, and that is how these items happened to be there. Generally speaking, the army following combat was never involved in collecting these kind of items. The only items they are interested in collecting is weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, the smuggled merchandise that was the subject of illegal trade, was that also the subject of confiscation and storing in these warehouses?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Most definitely, yes. That was another source of such goods.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3838, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How about motor vehicles belonging to the enemy. When they are seized, as well as other mobile property in possession of enemy formations, once they're seized are they also considered legitimate war booty?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the assets used by enemy during combat, if they stay behind after combat activities are finished constitute war booty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see document 17872, and this is under footnote 74 of your report. This document is dated the 11th of May, 1992, issued by the 30th Partisan Division. Can you please tell us what is being ordered by Colonel Tepsic in respect of motor vehicles and other assets?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This constitutes a hierarchical chain of command, that is to say the assistant for logistics from the corps conveys an order that the command of the 30th Division transfer part of the war booty to the corps depot, and he specifies here what is to be transferred and where. He is earmarking certain necessary assets that happened to be in the possession of the division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the attitude and how much attention was devoted by Mr. Brown to such orders and such items, and how does he explain items such parts of refrigerator, women's jackets and things? Did he ever establish how these items ended up in the war booty storehouse?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Some specific items such as mentioned under number 2, women's jackets and alike, what he did was that without any doubt put it into context and established a link with the civilian population, hence he concluded that this unit, the 30th Division, confiscated these items from non-Serb civilians in their zone of responsibility, which is impossible to infer from any document that was available.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 3839, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us briefly look at what the commander of the 30th Partisan Division is ordering or, rather, cautioning, if it is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have D00576 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who has issued this warning, and what is the essence of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 30th Division, the then-Colonel Galic, is warning the commanders of subordinate units at all levels to spare no effort to prevent looting, burning, and small private wars being waged in the area of the division, to provide protection for the refugees and the innocent civilians, and the enemy troops who surrendered ought to be treated in conformity with the international law governing the treatment of prisoners. All the violators of this order shall be subject to the most stringent legal measures, including physical execution. So basically this is a very radical order that he issued to his own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Mr. Brown's paragraph 2.182, goes on to say that the corps was being reported to by the 6th Krajina Brigade from Sanski Most, that there -- they were having serious problems with individuals involved in smuggling, robbery, and war profiteering, and that they had utilised a large number of cars and trucks which had been confiscated from the Muslims in the area. That's his footnote 162 [as interpreted]. In your document it is footnote 75.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we have in e-court 65 ter 05179.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us -- say item 5. Can we have the next page. This is dated the 6th of December, 1992, and page 5 -- or, rather, item 5 is on the next page. And in English on page 5. You mentioned the requisitioning of vehicles a moment ago. Was the owner entitled to receiving a receipt and an indemnity in case of his vehicle being requisitioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The duty to allow one's property to be requisitioned was an obligation just as conscription was. Holders of property were obliged, if required, to make their property available to the military forces. In return, they would receive a certificate to that effect, and in the event of the property getting damaged or destroyed, they were entitled to receiving proper compensation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at item 5, situation on the ground. What does paragraph 1 say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: "In the territory of Sanski Most municipality, the Muslims and Croats are calm and not creating any problems. They accept all measures undertaken by the authorities. However, major problems are groups of armed Serbs on the ground who are terrorising Muslims and Croats, looting everything in their way. There have also been killings, so that some of these groups have been arrested. There are a lot of cases involving smuggling, appropriation of vehicles, tractors, and so on."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't have to read out anything. Can you just tell us what item 7 applies to and does it contain the reason why vehicles were being requisitioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: What is discussed here is the condition in which these vehicles were. They were quite worn out by this time, not really in proper order, and it would be impossible to implement any assignments unless these were first repaired. And this was one of the reasons for requisitioning vehicles. This was to be done based on the needs and as they arose. Whenever their own vehicles would be damaged or be simply unserviceable, others would have to be requisitioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in Serb it says: "Freight vehicles and passenger vehicles were taken over from the Muslims." In English it reads that they were confiscated. Is there a difference between the term "taken over from" and "confiscated"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, "preuzet iz," "to take over from." Well, this is the legally provided process of hand-over, whereas "confiscation" means oftentimes "forcibly taken." That's what the word would mean in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3840, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection. Page 69, line 4, it identifies this document as Ewan Brown's footnote 162. That's either a typo or a translation error. It's actually 612, as well as 554. 612 is the one I think Mr. Karadzic was referring to when he began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think that I did say properly, but perhaps I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in chapter 5, item 39, paragraph 39, you address that part of Mr. Brown's report which deals with the destruction of religious facilities and the punishment of these incidents. In your report you cite D01979 - so it's a Defence exhibit; right? - as well as D01980. These are documents wherein the 1st Krajina Corps warns, demands, and prohibits the destruction of religious and cultural buildings. Have you ever established either on the basis of documents or reports or on the basis of anything else that legitimate military forces, regular military forces, allowed such activities or suppressed the fact that they had been done?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Nowhere in these documents can one find that the legal forces were engaged in the destruction of these buildings. There were instances of religious buildings having been destroyed, some through arbitrary conduct on the part of individuals and groups which cannot be in any way linked up with the regular military forces. There were also cases of abuse of religious buildings for military purposes, either as positions or sites from which fire was opened. As a result, such buildings became targets of attack. Nowhere did I find that anyone allowed, ordered, or instigated the destruction of religious properties. There were many documents, however, which highlighted the obligation to protect these same buildings regardless of their religious denomination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Republika Srpska consider all these buildings to be part of its heritage? Did you ever come across a document of mine where I forbade or ordered that these religious buildings be protected?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is one document of yours providing for the obligation to protect religious and cultural heritage. After all, it amounted to the heritage of the entire Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, can you tell us what Mr. Brown concluded about the relationship between the 1st Krajina Corps and the paramilitaries present in its area? What did you come to conclude about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: There were several examples such as the Wolves of Vucjak detachment and Veljko Ivanovic, the reconnaissance unit or the unit of scouts of Cigo Radanovic, Macko's unit, and similar. His conclusion was that the units' commands and other higher levels up the chain turned a blind eye or had this very reconciliatory attitude toward their unsoldierly, undisciplined, and at times rogue activity. Cases were cited such as the arrest of a colonel of the army, attack on a police station, and several other events. At this point Mr. Brown concluded his exploration of these relations and found that they were part and parcel of the Bosnian Serb forces, that they were part of the system, and that it was with the knowledge of the higher levels that they committed these misdeeds. However, what can be seen in the documents available is that in all the incidents cited, the perpetrators thereof were being punished and were punished. They were arrested, prosecute, and measures were taken against them. I do not deny the fact that these things happened, that the colonel, Chief of Staff of a Tactical Group who was involved in this event was really arrested by that one unit. However, measures were taken to bring him to justice. The same went for the attack against the Omarska Police Station and so on. It never happened that officially the authorities and army commands tolerated such displays of random behaviour, unsoldierly behaviour, and insubordination. This was not the practice and was not the system according to which the VRS worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In his paragraph 265, Mr. Brown says that although Talic prohibited those who were involved in these crimes from joining the corps, he says that certain paramilitary units mentioned by the Main Staff were nevertheless incorporated into the corps. Do you recall and do you know of our order which was admitted in this case prohibiting paramilitary formations from being set up and from being active and from being resubordinated to the army? Was it therefore to bring a paramilitary group into existence in fact a crime? They could not have joined the ranks of the regular army.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: For the most part it involved the misdeeds that the paramilitaries did against their own people, the Serbs primarily, against their own units. Or it was the case of them engaging in unlawful activities within units. There are no documents indicating that these units had committed certain war crimes for which they were then pardoned and allowed to resume their activity. They did display random and rogue behaviour at some point. However, through the orders of corps, they were deployed as individuals or groups, and they continued serving within army units. However, not a single individual in respect of whom there was a reason of suspicion that he committed a crime or who had been convicted or prosecuted could continue serving in the army through a decision issued by the authorities or the army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 65 ter 17792.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just two things briefly. If Mr. Karadzic could give me the reference he cited at page 73, line 20, "An order preventing paramilitaries from being resubordinated to the people," it says. And secondly, at page 73 at the top, the witness answered, "What can be seen in the documents available is that in all the incidents cited, the perpetrators were punished," et cetera. I don't know if Mr. Karadzic wants to tell us what documents we can find that in, or in each cases, in every incidence there was a prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that and now we're going to show a document, my document which placed a ban on the setting up and existence and activities of paramilitary formations. I ordered that they should be resubordinated and that was issued on the 3rd of June, 1992, and adopted on that date. However, I cannot give you a reference number. I can't give you the reference number of the exhibit, but I will be able to do that very soon. I would like to call up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With respect to the part of witness's answer, we may ask the witness if he could assist us. Do you remember your answer cited by Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Keserovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I remember. In the findings there is a citation. I can't give you the exact page because I don't know the findings by heart, but I'm sure there is a document which indicates that measures were taken against Milanovic, Radanovic, against Romanic. Those were individuals who had ties to paramilitary structures, and each of the documents states specifically what measures were ordered against each of the individuals.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope I'll find this. However, let me just show another document. Actually, say for the benefit of Mr. Nicholls that there are two documents: One is D1933, the other is D1993 [as interpreted], both issued on the 13th of June. One is a letter to Galic as report on the document, and the other document is the document itself placing a ban. One is D1933, and the other is D93.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, General, sir, if you can pay attention to bullet point 5 -- or paragraph 5, and can you tell us how that paragraph treats the behaviour of Lieutenant Milanovic? Number 5.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says here due to the incident that happened in 327th Motorised Brigade and extreme wilfulness and nonmilitary conduct of Lieutenant Milanovic and Captain Milanovic, investigative proceedings have been undertaken. This is one of the documents to support what I have just recently stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the nonmilitary conduct and wilfulness are breaches of discipline or crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: They can be breaches of discipline. However, extreme wilfulness and nonmilitary conduct are crimes. So they don't have to be misdemeanors at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3841, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2.70 in Mr. Brown's analysis, Mr. Brown believes that Milanovic could not stay as an officer in the corps. That's why I asked you what the sentence depends on. Is there any gradation in that? What does the severity of punishment depend on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to Mr. Milanovic personally, at that time, apart from what the unit did and then measures were ordered along the command responsibility lines, while he was serving in the army I -- while he participated in the war, he did not commit any acts for which he would have been deprived of his rank and removed from the army, for which he would have been dishonoured. It's just a matter of analysis whether it was possible to state that there were misdemeanors that had to be punished in that way. However, up to that time no foundations were found in the law for his dishonouring and from being removed in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are talking about what document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about 1772. It has been admitted. I apologise. For the participants, I would like to say that the issue of Cigo and Zolja is dealt in P02855 where a distinction is made between them and the group of robbers known as Suva Rebra and Skenovi [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in chapter 7 you mention something that Mr. Brown also dealt with, and that is connection between Pale and the Autonomous Region of Krajina. In your paragraph 43, you cite Mr. Brown's paragraph 1.113. In that paragraph he says that members of the ARK Crisis Staff were at times also given access to military and other detection facilities. He describes, based on an article in "Kozarski Vjesnik" a visit by the president of the Assembly, Mr. Vojo Kupresanin and members of the Crisis Staff to Manjaca camp. Could you please tell us how Mr. Brown treats that subject matter? What did he conclude, and what were his conclusions based on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Based on a relatively small number of documents of which one is a newspaper article, Mr. Brown ultimately concludes that the leadership, i.e., representatives of -- or individuals, members of the leadership of the ARK, had access but also that they had influence on the conditions and relationships in the camps or collection centres or investigative centres and that they exerted that immediate influence, i.e., that they could appear there as authorities. What various documents say is the fact that on those two occasions when individuals did appear in those camps, they went there to set somebody free from one of the camps, and on one occasion they escorted a commissary Mr. Mazowiecki, who was the representative of the international community. Based on that, nobody can draw a conclusion about their clear control or influence at that they exerted on the functioning of those places where people were incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can the witness be shown 65 ter 05578.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, during the 1.130 days of war, they made just a one-day visit, or perhaps they visited those place on two or three occasions for just one day. Would you see that as an influence exerted by ARK bodies on the prisons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't, especially in view of the fact that Manjaca prison camp was set up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's very leading. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've been very restrained today, but talking about 1.130 days of war when I think we all agree that Manjaca camp was closed in December 1992, when nobody could have visited it after that is a bit misleading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. This is the first omission on my part today. It was leading, but Batkovic existed throughout the war as a --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, talk about --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- camp accessible -- very well. I shall drop that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell us about the contents of this document which was issued on the 9th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report which speaks about the infiltration from the territory of the Republic of Croatia of a sabotage terrorist group into the area around Bosanska Gradiska. It also speaks about activities to fight that group and about the capturing of the group members. The document shows how the group was recruited and how they were sent across the Sava River in order to fight behind the Serbian lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brown mentions this document in his footnote 186. In paragraph 3 there is a reference to Manjaca. Can we go to the following page where a reference is made to Mazowiecki's visit, and I suppose Mr. Kupresanin was also there at the time. It's on the following page. It says on the previous page that the president of the Assembly of ARK. Who was the president of the ARK Assembly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Vojo Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that he gave some promises which were not founded. Did you know that Mr. -- okay. Let me not leading. On behalf of whom or what did Mr. Kupresanin visit these places and make promises?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin at that time could and most often did give statements on his own behalf if he had power of authority to do that. However, since Manjaca was under the control of the military, I believe that he could not do anything serious on his own. The only thing that I came across was his link with the central authorities, i.e., the authorities of Republika Srpska, whereby on one occasion he was authorised to visit the camp and to order -- or, rather, to convey some measures with regard to some of the detainees there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what detainee was in question and what measures were ordered?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was your decision that one of the MPs from the assembly from the ranks of the Muslim people had to be released with immediate effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, at page 79, line 25, where Mr. Keserovic -- General Keserovic states, "Mr. Kupresanin at that time could and most often did give statements on his own behalf if he had the power of authority to do that." I just wondered is that from documents or personal observation, because I didn't see it in the documents. I apologise if I missed it. In other words, was that as a fact witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The question was on behalf of whom or what did Mr. Kupresanin visit these places and make promises? What is your basis for your answer, Mr. Keserovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the screen we see a document which is a report, and according to that report he was a manager and gave some statements which were not founded. I did not come across any documents on which his authority could be founded, i.e., that he could give some statements of those kind -- of that kind. So there is no document that authorised him to do that. He could only provide statements on his own behalf.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D9273.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that you had access to this document. Can you tell us what is this document, and how does it relate to Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This is a record of 26 August, stipulating that an individual called Nedim Biscevic is released from the POW camp Manjaca and he was personally to be taken over by Mr. Vojo Kupresanin. So this is a document certifying that a person is being released from the prisoner of war camp. This was preceded by an order of the security chief of the 1st Krajina Corps, and I was one of its members at the time and we went there, made this arrangement and this person was eventually released from the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] aS well as the previous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 05 -- 05578 will be Exhibit D3842, and 1D9273 will be Exhibit D3843.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 00406.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about this document? Take a look at item 4. If we can scroll it up a bit, the Serbian version, so that we can see item 4. Can you tell us what this is all about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This is a combat report produced by the 1st Krajina Corps command. Under item 4 it is stated that in the area of the AR Krajina the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in Serbian, and we remain on the same page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several leaders and members of several parties in the AR of Krajina are clashing more and more with the official government of the SR BH. A boycott of deputies from the region attending the SR BH Assembly has been announced. And it has been demanded as an imperative that only Banja Luka can be the seat of the SR BH government." This document as well as some other reports that particularly dealt with the issue of morale demonstrates that at one point the army felt that there was disagreement between the leadership of the ARK and the authorities at the level of the republic. Given that everything that happens in politics, both good and bad things, reflects on the corps command, they decided to report this to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Has Mr. Brown noticed this, and did he pay any attention to this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: These disagreements were not the subject of Mr. Brown's attention in the sufficient measure. Now, speaking about relations between the ARK and the republican authorities, there were some objective circumstances that caused the communications to be almost completely severed, but there were also some subjective reasons as well which caused this rift as stated in the document. For almost two months the Krajina was cut off from the remaining part of Republika Srpska, i.e., the authorities in Pale, including telephone lines, and there was no corridor as well. So it was difficult to communicate with them. Similarly, the leadership of the ARK had their own vision, had their own ideas, but they not always coincided with the ideas of the central authorities and what the leadership in Pale thought. I cannot give you any specific details because this has to do with political conduct and not so much with military aspects, but I know that all of this stopped once the ARK ceased to exist in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection just because the answer wasn't completely clear about whether Mr. Brown had noticed this. It's his footnote 198 in Mr. Brown's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3844, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 484. If I could kindly ask for a extra five minutes and then we shall finish everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph are 1124, Mr. Brown emphasises that there were examples which demonstrate that even when there was interference by the civilian bodies in military matters the corps would often assist these bodies and so on. And then he goes on to say that General Talic was aware in early May that there were extremists in Kljuc and that also the president of the Kljuc municipality was -- attempted to command the units, hence he's asking the government of Krajina to intervene. And this is in his footnote 211. Can you tell us what that document is about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This document speaks about these extremely delicate relations between the civilian authorities and the military, particularly during the period while institutionally speaking all the mechanisms were not in place. There was still no transition from the properly ordered system in which the previous army existed and the new system that would be in force in this emerging state, and it was involved in parallel processes of setting up the army, the state, the government bodies, and is attempted to institutionalise all those processes. As I said, in conditions when the 4th Corps remained surrounded strategically was the reason why General Talic appealed to the political leadership that he had access to, that is to say the leadership of the ARK and not for reasons of disrespect for the central authorities. Now, as for the attempts in Kljuc on the part of the municipal leadership who tried to influence the commanding of the units was very ferociously stopped by General Talic and it was stopped, and they continued further on to carry out the orders issued by the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page item 3 in English, and we need the next page in Serbian, which speaks about murder committed by a person who was intoxicated, and it says that General Talic was aware of that. Can you tell us if General Talic undertook appropriate measures?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: A whole host of events took place in Kljuc that preceded an ultimate decision by the corps to place this area under their control. They first took over the relay, then JNA column was attacked and seven conscripts were killed in the attack, then there was an attack on another unit, there was an attack on a police patrol resulting in the death of one policeman, and all of this contributed to increasing the tension, and the corps was fully aware of that. Perhaps their response was somewhat belated because too many events of that nature happened before they decided to react.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3845, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last two documents, General. In chapter 8 you deal with the issue of paragraph 1132 in which he suggests that Mladic changed his opinion about the participation of non-Serbs in the army, police, government, company management, et cetera. You are challenging a document that I issued instead of the assembly, and in that regard can we have document 17873 under 65 ter. While waiting, General, can you tell me whether there were any Muslims and Croats in our army occupying high-ranking positions from the beginning of the war and whether there were any Muslim units that were fighting for Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were both individuals. I personally know that in the 1st Corps that we are analysing here there were not only Muslims and Croats, there were Slovenes and other ethnicities. We had one entire unit made up of Muslims called the independent unit Meso Selimovic, which was part of the 307th [as interpreted] Brigade from Derventa, and this unit was engaged throughout the war. In Eastern Bosnia Corps in the Semberija brigades we also had a unit composed of Muslims and also individual posts were held by both Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think you said 327th, not 307th.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 327th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in both versions. Item 2, page 7 in e-court. Page 7 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at paragraph 2 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: "Any sectarian attitude towards other ethnic groups should be eliminated if they accept our policy as stated above. They can be assigned work and other obligations to contribute to the development and advancement of the Serbian Republic. Everything else must be treated as treason and resistance to the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3846, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D04591. 1D04591. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is this official note about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This originated from the POW camp Manjaca, proposal to engage prisoners of war in war units, prisoners of war who had expressed desire to join units of the Army of Republika Srpska and to take part in its defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As I can see this, there are five Serb captives who want to fight.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, prisoners of war are everybody who found themselves to be on the opposite side, and that's how it happened that these Serbs were taken prisoner too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the proposal in the last passage regarding this sergeant, Radinovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It is proposed here with regard to Mesa Selimovic battalion that should they face problems by merging with other units to be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber who Mesa Selimovic was and what kind of unit it was that these Muslim volunteers were dispatched to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct, it has to do with the unit itself and not with the Mehmed Mesa Selimovic. Mehmed Mesa Selimovic was a prominent writer who said for himself that a Serb of Muslim confession. Now, the unit came into the being in the following way: The Derventa, Srbac, and Brod villages which were populated mostly by the Muslims, they expressed their loyalty to the Serb authorities and accepted what was reality at the time, and that was the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In return, their request was, and it was ultimately accepted, that they should be organised in a separate unit which was named Mesa Selimovic at their request. And they were part of, as I said, 327th Brigade, and they were listed within that brigade as an independent unit, and the unit was active within the brigade until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted and I would like to refer the parties to D479. This is my response to the Main Staff in relation to the wishes expressed by the Muslims and Croats - well, in this instance, the Muslims - to fight in our ranks, where I similarly said that they should be treated properly and fairly, that they should be assigned to available units and that they should not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- against the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unnecessary, Mr. Karadzic. It's already noted in his footnote. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3847, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you through your examination-in-chief, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. General, sir, thank you. I apologise for keeping you here for long. I offer this report into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it, General Keserovic, that it has been explained to you that the cross-examination by the Prosecution will take place next week.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I'm hearing of it for the next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My understanding is 9.00 on Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've schedule it actually for the 23rd of July. Unfortunately, and I apologise, members of our team failed to inform General Keserovic of this as they were instructed to do. So we apologise for that, and we have scheduled his cross-examination for Tuesday, the 23rd of July, and his arrival on the 22nd of July. We hope that that will work for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So he will go back and return.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. As I understood, he was not going to be cross-examined this week at all, and so he would have had to go back in any event. Since next week is full of witnesses, instead of rescheduling one of them, we decided it would be better if he came back the following week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does it suit you, General Keserovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the 23rd would definitely suit me more. However, I cannot possibly travel on the 21st, but I can on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There should be no problem with it. We will adjourn very shortly, but shall we discuss the scheduling. We have three witnesses for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it those three witnesses will be concluded by Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, sometime during the day on Wednesday we will finish with those three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which means that we may not have a hearing at all on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
